utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we are in open session again. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start asking questions of the witness, I would like the witness shown a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, is the information correct which you see before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like the witness to introduce himself with a little more detail to the Chamber. And that is the reason why the Defence is asking for a closed session for a few minutes, so that the witness can give more details to the Chamber about himself. This is his place of residence where he lived and where he worked before the conflict started and during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then turn into closed session so that the witness can give the details of his person. And then I take it that you indicate that we turn into open session again once we come to the real content of his testimony. We will now turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, you told us you lived in Sarajevo and you said where you lived. You explained to us that you lived in Sarajevo before the conflict broke out. I would like you to answer briefly when, according to you, that the conflict in Sarajevo started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean the start of the armed conflict? In my opinion, they started in early May 1992, after the incident in Dobrovoljacka Street. And if you mean when did the political conflict and all other conflicts start, they started by the nationalist parties, or we could call them chauvinist parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, when you tell us that in your opinion the armed conflicts started in May 1992, could you tell us within that political conflict which proceeded May, were there any incidents, in your opinion, that were pointing to armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the establishment of nationalist parties, through their exclusivity [as interpreted], and by intensively building hatred against other nations, other peoples, by the restoration of some symbols and insignia of the era of fascism, left a very bitter aftertaste in many people's mouth. Some very dark figures appeared who were using -- who were engaging in smuggling of currency and people said that they were engaging in armed smuggling. There were some verbal incidents, not only in the streets but also in the institutions, for instance, in the national Assembly where the representatives of the three nations insulted each other and were engaged in verbal duals. But the actual beginning of the conflict and the dark times in Sarajevo started with the first days in March when the murder occurred, the murder of a Serb occurred, and wounding of a priest, which rather made everybody upset, and also because the murderer was never found. It was that -- then that the first barricades was set up. And for me this is a material example, physical example, of the first ethnic division in Sarajevo, which preceded the political division of the city to two political options. Now, the events surrounding the lifting of the barricades which objectively delineated the areas where majority populations live, either the Muslim or the Serbian, the JNA tried to resolve this and sometimes they succeeded but mostly they did not. Because it was mostly in part blockade in its own actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, now, in your answer when you mentioned JNA, could you tell us if in the city of Sarajevo, you observed or did you see, were you an eyewitness to some activities of some soldiers belonging to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was unfortunately one of these citizens who still believed that the survival of the then-current state was still possible, and that the JNA, although it remained the only integral part of the state, that it was still in a position to prevent the conflicts which were being foreshadowed. Sarajevo had a specific situation, and I felt it as a realisation of two political consents. One which was in favour of destroying the old state and making new coalitions; and the second one which was trying to keep, reserve the old state, even in just verbal form. But the conditions were such that through the establishment of the nationalist parties, and there was also the formation of paramilitary and parapolice forces. At the time I wasn't really certain of this. But later on, particularly reading books and particularly the book by General Sefer Halilovic, I found out that it was already in the spring 1991, so that was one year before the war, that for the protection of the Muslim nation, of the Muslim people the, Patriotic League was established, which, as he writes in his book, had more than 160.000 people under arms. Now, I read this book. I don't know how many people under arms other parties had, but it is undeniable that very strange things happened. And one of the best examples that can be given is that in early March 1992, and as I still have problems with the throat, I was in the there then, for that reason, I was in the Military Hospital being treated by the then famous doctor Maksim Lucic, and he treated me. He was an acquaintance of my wife. And after the treatment or after the appointment was finished, he told me he was giving in terror, in fear, in panic because there was danger threatening from all sides. I asked what kind of danger. And then he took me to the window and he said that all of the residential buildings surrounding the Military Hospital, all of the walls had had holes in them, and he told me that the personnel of the Military Hospital is constantly being targeted, that behind these holes, there were armed people who were targeting staff of the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please give us more concise answers. We mentioned the Yugoslav People's Army. Would you tell us if you knew where the troops were stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had about six or seven barracks while the large ones was in the very heart of the city which I knew. There was a command at Bistrik. I believe it was the army command. There was the army centre and outside the city itself, they were still Lukavica called Viktor Bubanj and so. So there were enough of them. I believed they were strong enough to spare the city any conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I will go back to your earlier answer when you told us that you had gone to the army hospital, Military Hospital, and that you had been warned that the hospital was under siege, and it was observed by armed men. Did you learn at that time who were those armed men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everything was common knowledge. One knew of the Patriotic League, of the Green Berets, of the HOS, of the HVO, of the Serb forces, but they were all a part of the city where the population was Muslim. And it is quite evident, at least from what I could learn, that the Green Berets and the Patriotic League were about to encircle the city. And I learned from my friends, Muslim friends, that the end had come to the Federal Yugoslavia, that there was a plan which the Yugoslav People's Army would either lay down weapons or would be liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning you told us that in your mind -- to your mind, the conflict in Sarajevo started in early May. What armed conflict did you have in mind when you said that, "early May"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On television I saw -- it was a live transmission of events on Dobrovoljacka Street. After that, as far as I could make it out, two sides came in the being, that is two fronts, or rather one front with two enemies. And after that date, practically, that 1992, fighting did not stop. The fighting never stopped gaining and gaining momentum, and I think that it was that day that the proper conflict started between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP, you spoke -- you portrayed for us a period in Sarajevo, that is, March, April -- well, in May, too, in 1992. Can you tell us if during that time if you saw any armed men? Did you see any armed individuals and did you see soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: and troops were quartered. Can you tell us, please, if you used to see those soldiers and what kind of clothes did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was this coffee shop, and it was in the building that I lived in and almost daily --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question and the previous answer on this basis. The witness was invited to - I'm now quoting from line 17 - tell us if during that time, that's early 1992, you saw any armed men. The witness then described various facilities where he thought, at least in relation to an artillery unit, there were military units quartered, but did not explain how he came by that knowledge that he saw them or not. My learned colleague then said: "Witness, you lived in that area where you saw military facilities and troops were quartered." My objection is that the witness is giving information without making it clear what the source of that information is, whether it is his first-hand observations, or whether, as it seems, it is what he was told. He refers to a commander, I think, who lived in the same building as him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the objection is sustained. Would you please guide the witness in such a way that we know exactly what is the source of his information, what he saw, what he heard. And perhaps if you take a bit more of the lead, then it might be easier to do so. Please proceed. And may I tell you, you mentioned once the name of the street where you lived and that was dealt with in closed session. So measures will be taken that it is not on the record anymore. But may I remind you that it is in your own interest that these protective measures are put in place and perhaps also for you, Ms. Pilipovic, to put your questions in such a way although it was, I would say, rather spontaneous, that the witness mentioned a name, that you keep in mind that what you don't want to be disclosed to the public, will not be disclosed to the public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But I have to say that my next question was whether the witness saw these armed men, and that is why I will ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you said -- when you told us about the places where, according to you, there were soldiers, can you tell us if you personally saw those places and soldiers in them. That is, do you know it of your own? Do you have direct knowledge of it or were you told about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes. And after all, it lasted so long that whoever wanted to could easily see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you saw them and that it lasted long, can you tell us from when, that is, when did you begin to see? When did you start seeing soldiers in those places that you listed? That is, men who, according to you, were soldiers, and what made you conclude that they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except in the dentistry school, that was a unit which came later, all those other places existed from the very beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us "from the very beginning of the conflict," can you be more precise and tell us which month 1992? I believe you have 1992 in mind. It is in 1992 that you started seeing soldiers there, when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginnings of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that from the beginning of May 1992 in the part of the city where you lived, you used to see soldiers, can you describe to us what they looked like? Did they wear uniforms? What uniforms? Did they have any insignia and whether they bore arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers who were under the command of Juka Prazina had black uniforms. Soldiers whose commander was a commander whom I had mentioned wore camouflage uniforms. There were soldiers in some units who were orange uniforms, red uniforms. I mean, those were early days of the war yet, so a large number of different units and all that I can say is that is how I saw them. Weapons whenever Jusuf Pusina went, they were armed men accompanying him with -- automatic rifles --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you that when you speak to speak in the microphone so that those who are interpreting your words can better understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP1, you described to us, according to you, soldiers wearing specific uniforms and weapons. Did you also see around the city of Sarajevo any men wearing civilian uniforms, that is, who were -- who looked like civilians yet were under arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "yes," can you tell us when and where did you used to see such men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As early as the latter half of April. And especially in the early days of May, men bearing weapons searched houses, entered, looked for those who allegedly held weapons. Yes, I came across such people. I came across those men at checkpoints, because as soon as the conflict broke out, checkpoints were set up. And there were also men wearing civilian clothes but under arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness DP1, when you described the part of the city that you lived in and places where you saw armed men, that is, troops, were there any other places of which you had -- which were used by the army, according to what you had direct knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that time I didn't go around the city. I moved only from my home to my place of work in the beginning. That was in the beginning. And later home from my home to a place where I could find some food and back. So yes, I heard about it, but having in mind the objection, I do not have any direct knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the building that you lived in, were there any troops there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In early August, Jovan Divjak, at that time he was Deputy Commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, came to the building and convened a meeting of people who lived there and who, in a way, ran various companies, and suggested and then ordered that the ground floor, the first floor, be vacated of the employees because of the general headquarters, that is, the Supreme Command headquarters would be there. And that is how it was. It was vacated and part of the army came in, that is, their Supreme Command. So I stopped going there after a while, but in order they were there, they stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that lower floors were vacated and that the army took over the lower floors of the building that you worked in, are you telling us that you went on working there, and which floors did you use when you came to work?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It may be a translation problem. The question directed the witness's attention to the building in which he lived, but it seems unclear to me, having regard to the answer, whether that was the building in which he lived or the building in which he worked. The next question, that is the last question by my learned colleague, refers to the building in which he worked. Perhaps that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic. It looks as if your question in the English transcript it is page 69 line 16, it says: "In the building that you lived in, were there any troops there?" And it seems from the answer and your next question that it was the building in which you worked. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I think that is how I asked my question. Perhaps it was misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it is clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. DP1, you are telling us that the first two floors or three, as you told us, were the floors of the building that you worked in, and that is where the troops were put up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The troops -- the army established control at the entrance, but that is a six-storey building and the employees could go in and climb up to their offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. DP1, since we are talking about the army and armament, can you tell us if in the part of the city where you lived and where you saw troops, did you also used to see weapons, and if you did, what kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said that I saw armed men and armed soldiers, as far as I can identify the time. It is not easy to recall, but when the Prime Minister changed, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when Mr. Siljadzic took up the post, I think it was then that soldiers moved -- that until then, the soldiers moved mostly around town without weapons. But as of that time, they began bearing -- began carrying weapons around.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that, can you please be more specific as to the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it must have been after September 1992, but I can't really be more precise -- perhaps even later.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you if in that part of the city where you used to see armed troops and armed men, I asked you if you also saw some weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Weapons, small and big weapons, if I understand what you mean, both small firearms and artillery. Of the latter, it is only one, one mortar, that mortar was mounted on a truck. It moved through the city, but it is quite certain that there were also other pieces. I can speak only about places that were shelled frequently, that is an assumption that is where the artillery pieces were, and it was somewhere below Kosevo hill. People used to say - how shall I put it - that some mortars, artillery pieces were of some mounted at the railway station in carriages --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. Again, this is evidence of what he heard people say, rather than what he saw. And my objection is that this evidence is of little assistance to the Trial Chamber. The first part of his answer, I don't object to, that is he saw personally a truck that had a mortar mounted on to it. And beyond that point, the witness himself refers to his evidence being an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, part of the reason is that you objected to the answer rather than the question, and that's -- but perhaps I -- we could find a way out. Ms. Pilipovic -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can I just say that the question was not objectionable, that is why I didn't object to it. The question invited the witness to respond if he saw some weapons, and he went beyond the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you will understand, that, first of all, hearsay is not, as such, prohibited in this Tribunal. On the other hand, Ms. Pilipovic, you will also understand that if hearsay is not about specific events but rather general, and the sources of the hearsay are also very general, that of course makes it less likely that when assessing the probative value of the testimony that it scores very high. I would say that is a lesson of experience in general. So therefore, if you would guide the witness -- of course, you did so, but perhaps also by interfering in his answers. If you think that he could give better details, even if it was hearsay, then that certainly would assist the Chamber. And for the witness, I would like to tell you that this Chamber and the parties are mainly interested to hear what you observed by yourself. That does not mean that something that you heard from other people might be relevant -- would be irrelevant, it might be very relevant. But if you please listen carefully to the questions put to you and try to answer as much as you can and what you know from your own experience your own observation, and if there is any specific aspect that you have not of direct observation, you certainly can tell us, but Ms. Pilipovic, then you can perhaps ask in more detail what is the source of the knowledge of the witness. Please proceed. I say "please proceed," but it is 7.00. So for that reason, we perhaps better not proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was about to ask him that after he has given us his answer, that was to be my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we do that tomorrow then. Mr. DP1, your examination has only just started. It will be continued tomorrow. We will start again at a quarter past 2.00. You also are supposed to have not any direct contact with the parties that are examining you at this very moment. So we hope to see you back tomorrow. What I had forgotten to say in the beginning of your testimony is that whatever we were informed that you might have some health problems, if that occurs, don't hesitate to inform us. I know that everything has been put in place in order to make sure that whenever you have difficulties that you will be assisted in a proper way to overcome these difficulties. So do not hesitate if that would occur. Then I would like to inform the parties just for one second about another issue but, Madam Usher, could you perhaps please escort the witness out of the courtroom in such a way that the face distortion will still be effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I would like to inform the parties about is about the court schedule. It is the understanding that the parties would rather do the morning sessions rather than the afternoon sessions, am I correct, or would you in general terms prefer the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, speaking entirely for myself, I find the alternative weeks of assistance with domestic arrangements, but clearly that is not the determining factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I inform the parties then in the week of the 21st of October, at the 21st, the 22nd, and if we are sitting, and that's not for sure yet, the 25th - because we are not scheduled for that day as far as I can see - but at least on the 21st and 22nd of October, we could sit in the morning. Then in the week of the 4th of November, on from Tuesday, that means from the 5th of November up to the 8th of November, we would have an opportunity to sit in the morning as well. And the same is probably true for the week of the 2nd of December, that means the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th and the 6th of December, since we are not sitting on the 5th. I would like to -- the parties to check in their agenda as to whether there is any obstacle for sitting in the mornings during these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Just one thing. General Galic whispered to me for reasons that have to do with his health, he would also rather that we sit in the mornings, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we have to weigh the health problems and the domestic problems -- well, quite a lot of problems. I would not spend too much time on it at this very moment, because we have to finish now. But I gave the dates, and if you would consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one other housekeeping matter we have not received from the Defence the list of exhibits and witnesses for next week giving the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven-day term, yes. I would like to be informed right at the beginning of tomorrow morning when the Defence will serve the next week programme, or whether it has already been served upon them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will submit it in one hour. I guess not later than an hour. Perhaps it has already arrived because we issued instructions to our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will have a copy then as well. And I hope that protective measures are always indicated on that list, if not, please make sure that it is clear to everyone whether the protective measures are sought in respect of that witness. Since it is 5 minutes past 7.00 already, and if there is nothing really urgent, I would adjourn until tomorrow quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.06 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of October, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
